cards.explanation: The answer is True, friends. Verse 1 says His disciples were hungry, so they began to pick the heads of grain and eat them. It's like grabbing a cookie off the cooling rack when your stomach starts growling. Hold onto that snack, because somebody is about to have a LOT to say about it.

The answer is that they're doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath, friends. The Pharisees, a group of religious leaders, say, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.” They bring it straight to Jesus about His disciples. The day they name is the Sabbath.

The answer is into the house of God, friends. Jesus says David entered the house of God. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), went in with his hungry companions and they ate the consecrated bread. Jesus pulls an example out of Scripture instead of just arguing. I think that's a clever way to answer people who say they know the rules.

The answer is priests, friends. Jesus says the consecrated bread was not lawful for David and his companions to eat, but only for the priests. And they ate it anyway. Jesus uses that moment from Scripture to answer the Pharisees.
The answer is False, friends. Jesus says, “…the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent?” He asks whether they haven't read that in the Law. The word He uses is innocent.

The answer is One greater than the temple, friends. Jesus says, “But I tell you that One greater than the temple is here.” He just talked about the priests serving in the temple, and now He says there's One greater. That is a big claim, and He says it plainly.

The answer is innocent, friends. Jesus says, “If only you had known the meaning of ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent.” He uses the word innocent for the ones the Pharisees had condemned. It's the same word He used about the priests a moment earlier.

The answer is Sabbath, friends. Jesus says, “For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.” Son of Man is a name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). The Pharisees brought up the Sabbath, and Jesus finishes by saying who is Lord of it.

The answer is accuse, friends. Verse 10 says, “In order to accuse Jesus, they asked Him…” The text names accusing as their purpose for the question. And the man with the withered hand was right there in the synagogue while they asked.

The answer is that he will take hold of it and lift it out, friends. Jesus asks, “…will he not take hold of it and lift it out?” Nobody stands at the edge of a pit checking the calendar first. Jesus uses that picture to make His point about the Sabbath.
The answer is valuable, friends. Jesus says, “How much more valuable is a man than a sheep!” He just talked about lifting a sheep out of a pit. Then He says a man is worth much more than that.

The answer is True, friends. Jesus says, “Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” He says it right after the sheep in the pit and the value of a man. That's His answer to the question about healing.

The answer is “Stretch out your hand,” friends. Jesus says that to the man with the withered hand. That's all He says, and the man does it. I'd love to know how it felt to stretch out that hand, but the text doesn't say, so I'll just guess it was something.
The answer is False, friends. The man stretched out his hand and it was restored to full use, just like the other. So it wasn't a half fix. The whole hand was made right, matching the other one.

The answer is True, friends. Verse 14 says the Pharisees went out and plotted how they might kill Jesus. A man just got his hand restored, and this is how they responded. I think this part is heavy, so we'll let it be heavy.

The answer is that He withdraws from that place, friends. Verse 15 says, “Aware of this, Jesus withdrew from that place.” He knew about the plot and He left. The text doesn't give a reason beyond that, so I'll leave it at that.
The answer is True, friends. Verse 15 says large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all. Not some of them. All of them, and the crowds were large.

The answer is not to make Him known, friends. Verse 15 says He healed them all, and then verse 16 says He was “…warning them not to make Him known.” The text doesn't give His reason in that verse. Matthew moves right on to the words of Isaiah.

The answer is False, friends. The words from Isaiah, the prophet, say, “He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets.” So the Servant doesn't quarrel and doesn't cry out. A very different kind of loud from the one I use at my ovens.

The answer is that He will not break or extinguish them, friends. The words say, “A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish…” Most of us would snuff out a wick that's barely glowing. These words say the Servant won't.

The answer is hope, friends. The last line says, “In His name the nations will put their hope.” Hope is a good place to land. These words start with a chosen Servant and end with the nations hoping in His name.
